ORIGINAL ARTICLE
OtoVision: Bridging machine learning and edge computing for effective and affordable ear disease diagnosis
Rishit Yokananth1 • Varun Gosula2
Received: 25 June 2024 / Accepted: 28 August 2024 / Published online: 28 November 2024  The Author(s) 2024
Abstract The primary aim of this research is to tackle the issue of inaccurate and inconsistent ear disease detection, particularly in remote and under-resourced areas. Traditional diagnostic methods employed by general practitioners and otolaryngologists have shown limitations, underscoring the need for more reliable approaches in these challenging healthcare environments. In response to this issue, a digital otoscope powered by the Rockchip RK3566 processor and enhanced with machine learning capabilities has been developed. This device, using a novel camera system, captures high-resolution images of the patient’s ear and applies image classification algorithms to identify and categorize various ear conditions in real time. The design of OtoVision emphasizes ease of use, affordability, and adaptability to different healthcare settings, aiming to make advanced diagnostic tools more accessible to underserved populations. Our testing and analysis reveal that OtoVision significantly enhances the accuracy of ear disease diagnosis. In controlled settings, the device achieved an accuracy rate of approximately 87% when connected to a desktop computer and 82% when operating on a standalone Rockchip single- board computer. These results indicate a substantial improvement over traditional diagnostic methods and demonstrate the potential of integrating machine learning technologies into medical diagnostics. OtoVision represents a step forward in the field of medical diagnostics, particularly for the detection of ear diseases in areas where specialist care is scarce. By leveraging machine learning and digital imaging, OtoVision offers a more accurate, accessible, and cost-effective solution compared to conventional methods. Ongoing development will focus on conducting extensive field testing.
Keywords Artificial intelligence  Biomedical engineering  Deep learning  Edge computing  Machine learning
1 Introduction
The necessity for improved ear disease detection, particu- larly in remote and under-resourced settings, is an urgent call for modern healthcare systems. The current diagnostic practices, usually carried out by general practitioners who are often the first line of defense for individuals presenting with symptoms related to auditory pathology, face incon- sistency and inaccuracy. This discrepancy is evident in Pichichero et al.’s study, which reported a concerning 25% discrepancy between the diagnosis made by general
practitioners and those made by otolaryngology specialists [1]. Furthermore, pediatricians’ correct diagnosis rate was a mere 50% compared to the 73% accuracy rate of oto- laryngologists [2]. These studies underscore the need for innovative and effective solutions to inaccurate diagnoses.
Recent strategies to address diagnostic challenges in otology increasingly rely on digital otoscopy, a tool that has become more prevalent due to its effectiveness. Digital otoscopes offer features like replay-video playback or frame-by-frame analysis, enhancing the learning experi- ence for medical students. In contrast, traditional medical otoscopes, while widely used, are often prohibitively expensive. This high initial cost limits their accessibility, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. For instance, while full-size otoscopes typically cost around $250, digital video otoscopes can start at $1000, making them unaffordable for many consumers and healthcare facilities in underprivileged areas [3, 4].

Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) and its subset, machine learning (ML), have emerged as promising areas of exploration. Machine learning’s primary applications encompass clustering, feature identification, pattern recognition, classification, and prediction [5]. With the growing availability of healthcare and medical data [6], AI and ML have been integrated into various aspects of medical practice to enhance patient services, disease detection, and treatment methods [7]. An essential appli- cation of machine learning in healthcare is medical image classification, often achieved through neural networks, specifically, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [5, 8]. This has ushered in a new era of machine learning-aided medical devices, which promise improved clinical prac- tices and cost-efficiency [9].
Drawing upon these developments in digital otoscopy and machine learning, we propose OtoVision, a Radxa Rockchip RK3566-powered digital otoscope enhanced by machine learning. The Rockchip RK3566 platform, renowned for its compactness, affordability, and flexibility, has proven to be a revolutionary tool in medical device prototyping. Its ability to process medical images, handle low-contrast images, and reduce noise has great potential in image classification ML applications. Leveraging these advantages, OtoVision seeks to introduce a new paradigm in ear disease detection and diagnosis.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Sect. 2 provides a comprehensive review of our machine learning algorithm and its applications such as our dataset. Sect. 3 describes the development of OtoVision Digital Otoscope Device and the experimental design methodol- ogy used to test the efficacy of our solution. Section 4 presents the results of our experiment, followed by Sect. 5 where we discuss our findings and their implications. Section 6 concludes the paper, summarizing our work and outlining potential directions for future research. Lastly, Sect. 7 outlines the data availability of our work, with Sect. 8 listing the references used within this paper.
2 Machine learning applications
In the domain of machine learning, we adopted deep learning to establish an effective Python algorithm for detecting ear diseases. This algorithm efficiently classifies images into five categories—COM, Earwax, Myringosclerosis, Normal, and OME—with remarkable accuracy.
To provide a foundation for this algorithm, we compiled an extensive dataset of otoscope images sourced from multiple open-access datasets. These datasets, originally used for independent otoscopy-based machine learning research in peer-reviewed journals, were made available to
the public through repositories such as Zenodo and Fig- share. In our dataset, 880 images came from the University of Chile Hospital Dataset [10]. Another 784 images were from eligible patients examined at Van Akdamar Hospital in Turkey [11]. Finally, 339 images were from primary care clinics at Ohio State University (OSU) used for the OtoMatch Study [12]. Not all images from each dataset were used due to the specificity of classes in our study. Our final dataset included 2003 otoscope images (as shown in Fig. 1), with the average image height and width being 501.7 and 540.1. This resulted in a uniform aspect ratio of 0.9 across our compiled dataset. The dataset was split into training, validation, and testing sets, with the training set comprising 70% (1398 images) of the total dataset. The remaining 30% was equally divided into validation and testing sets, each containing 15% of the dataset. The training dataset included varying classes of ear conditions: Otitis Media with Effusion (OME) for 125 images, Earwax for 252, Normal for 653, Myringosclerosis for 170, and Chronic Otitis Media (COM) for 198.
A unique advantage of integrating different open-access datasets is the diversity in image resolutions. The Chilean dataset predominantly featured images with a resolution of 420 9 380 pixels, the Turkish dataset focused on a square format of 500 9 500 pixels, and the Ohio dataset had more variable resolutions (but hovered around 585 9 740 pix- els). The diversity in resolutions introduced an implicit form of data augmentation, forcing the algorithm to become adept at recognizing patterns across various scales and dimensions. As a result, this helps improve the model’s generalization capabilities by making it more robust to unseen data. Additionally, this also reduces the likelihood of overfitting, where the model performs well on training data but poorly on new, unobserved data. Thus, our model and dataset are more effective and reliable in real-world applications.
Our model employs the EfficientNetB5 convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, which was proposed by Tan and Le [13]. EfficientNetB5 is constructed with a diverse set of layers, including convolutional layers, sep- arable depthwise convolutional layers, and fully connected layers. This CNN architecture stands out by uniformly scaling network dimensions—depth (number of layers),

width (number of neurons per layer), and resolution (input image size)—through a method called compound scaling, optimizing both learning capacity and computational effi- ciency. The compound scaling employs a coefficient to uniformly scale these dimensions from the base model (EfficientNetB0) to larger variants such as EfficientNetB5, where the coefficient is 5. The scaling is guided by the formula depth: aU, width: bU, resolution: cU (for example, depth: a5, width: b5, resolution: c5 for EfficientNetB5). Here, U is an exponent that can be adjusted based on computational resources and desired model size, while a, b, and c are constants derived from the EfficientNetB5 model. The architecture incorporates inverted bottleneck convolutions (MBConv) akin to MobileNetV2, followed by depthwise convolutions, to efficiently minimize computa- tional load.
In the architecture of EfficientNetB5, a standout feature is the Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) block, which signifi- cantly enhances the model’s capability to handle high- resolution image classification. The SE block’s primary function is to recalibrate channel-wise feature responses dynamically. It does this by selectively emphasizing informative features and suppressing less useful ones, enabling the network to concentrate on the most important aspects of the input data. This targeted recalibration is critical in complex tasks like identifying subtle yet crucial patterns in high-resolution images. Moreover, Effi- cientNetB5 incorporates skip connections, which aid in efficient network training by allowing direct gradient propagation through the network. This helps in maintaining a steady flow of information and gradients, essential for deep network training. The synergy between the SE block and skip connections is a key contributor to the model’s enhanced accuracy. Figure 2 details the EfficientNetB5 model’s workflow, including preprocessing, feature map
generation, convolution and pooling layers, fully connected (FC) layers, and the normalization of raw predictions (logits), illustrating the integral role of these components in efficient image classification.
In the initial parts of the Python algorithm, there was preprocessing and classification of ear images into distinct classes. We adhered to a 70%, 15%, and 15% split for training, testing, and validation data, respectively. The data were resized to fit EfficientNetB5’s requirement of 456 9 456 pixels, using bicubic interpolation to preserve image quality. Data augmentation included rotations of up to ± 15 degrees, height and width shifts of up to 10%, horizontal flips, and brightness adjustments within a range of ± 20%. These techniques were chosen to mimic real- world variability and enhance model robustness. Impor- tantly, all preprocessing steps, including resizing, feature extraction, and augmentation, were conducted indepen- dently of the validation dataset. The validation dataset remained completely untouched by any algorithm to pre- vent data leakage and ensure that the model’s accuracy was not artificially inflated.
In the context of our model, normalization was crucial for managing the varying lighting conditions and color distributions present within our ear image dataset. Pixel values were scaled to a range of [0, 1] based on the mean and standard deviation of the training set, with normal- ization applied separately to both the training and valida- tion datasets to prevent data leakage. Additionally, Group Normalization was implemented within our EfficientNetB5 architecture to replace Batch Normalization. This change was necessary due to the dependency of Batch Normal- ization on batch size, which led to unstable estimates of mean and variance with smaller batches, introducing sig- nificant accuracy problems during model deployment. Group Normalization, in contrast, did not depend on batch size and normalizes across channels, effectively handling features ranging from simple color contrasts to more complex textures and shapes.
To address class imbalances within our dataset, we applied class weighting during the training phase. This ensured that each class was fairly represented in the loss function, preventing the model from becoming biased toward more prevalent classes. The combined effects of these preprocessing steps—careful normalization and class weighting—contributed to the model’s stability, general- ization ability, and overall accuracy, leading to substantial improvements during deployment.

3 Development and methodology
3.1 Device development
OtoVision’s software ecosystem is structured around an accurate machine learning model paired with a graphical user interface (GUI): both tailored for the precise diagnosis of ear pathologies. As described in the previous section, the ML model is developed in Python, uses extensive training processes, and has a diverse dataset of otoscopic images to ensure high accuracy and reliability in real-world appli- cations. Once the training was completed, the model was saved and exported into a.h5 file, which facilitates its deployment and integration onto the OtoVision software.
Complementing the machine learning is OtoVision’s GUI, constructed through the PyQt5 framework to offer an interactive interface to users. The initial screen presents a live video stream from the otoscope, which is a critical feature for clinicians to perform and view ear examinations in real time. The GUI allows for interactive engagement with the stream, such as pausing, resuming, and capturing a picture. The GUI also integrates an ‘‘analyze’’ function that interprets the video feed using the machine learning model to provide immediate diagnostic predictions as shown in Fig. 3. Beyond this, the GUI’s ‘‘analytics’’ section contains previously captured images with their predictions and probability distributions. The system is also designed with multiple users in mind, offering personalized settings and account management features that enable a tailored expe- rience especially useful in medical settings.
To power the machine learning and GUI in the OtoVi- sion digital otoscope, a powerful and compatible single- board microcomputer was identified: Radxa Rockchip RK3566 Compute Module 3. This is a microcomputer using Debian OS, with its drivers deemed compatible with the PyQt5 GUI and the OV2740 endoscopic camera module described below. The Rockchip RK3566 operates on the Radxa CM3 processor, featuring a quad-core Arm Cortex-A55 CPU clocked at 1.8GHz and an Arm Mali- G52-2EE GPU. Offering versatility, it supports a range of configurations for LPDDR4 RAM (1/2/4/8GB) and eMMC storage (0/8/16/32/64/128 GB). These robust specifications position the Rockchip RK3566 as an optimal single-board computer, delivering enhanced processing power, efficient
performance, and seamless compatibility for our digital otoscope. Additionally, a Waveshare 4-inch HDMI LCD, with a 800 9 480 resolution, IPS display, and touchscreen, was used with the Rockchip RK3566 to display the GUI.
Through the prototyping process, instead of using a modular camera system, a small custom endoscopic camera module was determined to be the best course of action. The OV2740 endoscope camera, with its cost-effectiveness and inclusion of LEDs, was determined to be the best camera for its price and ability to avoid visual obstruction. After choosing this camera, a custom camera module (including PCB’s for both the LED’s and camera module) was created to house the OV2740 camera and sensor (HC-OV2740) as well as to integrate it with the microcomputer. This camera has high-quality specifications such as a resolution of 1920 9 1080 pixels, a frame rate of 60 fps, and a default field of view of 80 without distortion. These features, coupled with the camera’s 2.07 MP optical format on a 1/6- inch sensor, make the OV2740 an exemplary imaging solution for our otoscope.
In the final stage of development, a main PCB was precisely engineered and placed in the otoscope’s top compartment (Fig. 4). This PCB features connectors compatible with the Rockchip RK3566. It also includes an HDMI port for the Waveshare 4-inch HDMI LCD, crucial for displaying the GUI. A USB type 3.1 connector is integrated for connecting the OV2740 camera module. Additionally, the PCB features an SD card slot to house the SD card containing the GUI and machine learning model, along with a DC adapter to power the entire setup. 3.2 Testing methodology
The testing process was carefully designed to validate the performance and robustness of our machine learning model. The study took place on a high-performance Mac- Book workstation with an M1 Pro chip. For the computa- tional procedures involved in the testing, the Jupyter notebook platform running Python was chosen. Figure 7 outlines the workflow of the OtoVision system, showcasing each computational step from data collection to final classification.
Evaluation metrics were crucial in this study. The model’s performance was assessed using a series of pivotal indicators. The training accuracy was measured to capture the model’s grasp of the patterns within the training data. In parallel, the testing accuracy was monitored, providing insights into how the model responds to unfamiliar data. For a deeper dive into these accuracy metrics, a classifi- cation report and a confusion matrix were employed. These analytical tools offered a careful understanding of the

across varied data points. Upon concluding the training and internal validation on the computer, the trained model was exported in a ’.h5’ file format. This format encapsulates the entire model architecture, coupled with its learned weights.
Following this, two pivotal testing phases were con- ducted. Initially, a designated testing folder, with new images untouched during the training or validation pro- cesses, was used to assess the model’s performance on the computer. After assessing the outcomes on the computer, the testing transitioned to its next crucial phase: deploy- ment and evaluation on the Rockchip RK3566. This second testing phase is important since it offers a lens into the model’s performance under the constraints of a different and lower-performance hardware environment, epitomiz- ing OtoVision’s anticipated operational conditions. Ensuring a consistent evaluation methodology, the previ- ously mentioned untouched testing folder was once again utilized. In addition, to further validate the model’s robustness and versatility, open-source images from Goo- gle Images (that were not part of the original dataset) that spanned the five classes were incorporated into the testing procedure, ensuring a comprehensive evaluation. To com- plement these evaluations and showcase the quality of our imaging system, detailed images of the tympanic mem- brane captured by the OV2740 powered camera module are presented in Fig. 8, demonstrating the device’s ability to capture clear images. Additionally, Fig. 9 displays the successful deployment of the machine learning model on the new open-source images from Google Images.

the first deployment phase on the Macbook workstation after running the machine learning model. The deployment process was done using the.h5 file from the ML model and a deployment python script file, as predictions were made using the images in the untouched testing folder. As dis- played by the confusion matrix for this run (Fig. 10), there were effective classification outcomes for COM, Earwax, and Normal. However, classes such as OME and Myringosclerosis displayed less accurate prediction results, showcasing areas where the model may benefit from enhancements.
After using the Macbook workstation, the study shifted its focus to the Rockchip RK3566 for deployment within the OtoVision device. The Rockchip RK3566 used a deployment process similar to what would be done within the GUI and the general workflow detailed previously. The.h5 and deployment python script files were used to make predictions on the Rockchip RK3566 board using images in the untouched testing folder and Google Images. As the model had never seen these images before, it is the most efficient way to test the device when patient testing is not available.
When assessed on the Rockchip RK3566, the model exhibited a precision of 78%, test accuracy of 82%, and an F1 score of 79%. A confusion matrix was generated for this run as well (Fig. 11). Expectedly, due to the model’s initial training data, prediction inefficiencies for the OME and Myringosclerosis classes persisted. When compared with the MacBook workstation, the Rockchip’s restricted hard- ware capabilities slightly hindered the model’s accuracy. Nevertheless, the testing accuracy remained impressive, surpassing 80%—an accuracy surpassing conventional physician’s diagnoses. This high accuracy can be attributed to the model’s robustness against discrepancies in image resolutions sourced from varied online platforms (re- siliency) and the use of Group Normalization as previously discussed.
5 Discussion
While our machine learning model has demonstrated a commendable level of precision in classifying various ear conditions, obtaining a testing accuracy of 87%, there is a marked disparity in its performance across the different disease classes. Certain conditions, such as Otitis media with effusion (OME) and myringosclerosis, posed greater challenges, potentially due to their complex and subtle visual attributes. This variability in performance offers an area for future improvements, primarily through model refinement targeted at these specific conditions. The deployment of the model on a Rockchip device, while successful, yielded a slight dip in accuracy to 82%. The
reduction in accuracy when transitioning from a MacBook workstation to a Rockchip RK3566 was expected. This can be attributed to the relative hardware constraints of the Rockchip, emphasizing the ongoing challenge in edge computing of balancing model performance optimization with hardware capabilities. Additionally, the pronounced class imbalance in our dataset can pose a challenge to our model’s effectiveness, and addressing this as recent studies suggest could help improve accuracy [14]. Despite this, it is worth noting that the model still achieved an accuracy rate that surpasses a general physician diagnosis, under- scoring its potential utility in real-world scenarios. This is due to the fact that studies have shown that general physicians have limited accuracy, with around 75% accu- racy at best [15]. Additionally, the accuracy rate that pediatricians diagnose AOM and OME is 50%, whereas otolaryngologists diagnose these diseases with 73% accu- racy [15].
The deployed model showed resilience when handling images of varying resolutions found in our testing dataset, still maintaining a high level of accuracy. This suggests that the model has the potential to properly handle real- world scenarios, such as telemedicine and remote health- care settings where the image quality may vary due to different conditions. The robustness of the model could also be tested with a larger and more diverse dataset. This would not only help assess the generalizability and scala- bility of the model but also potentially contribute to improving its performance.
While there have been studies focusing on ear disease detection using machine learning models, none of them have advanced to the point of creating a unique digital otoscope diagnostic tool. This represents a significant stride forward in the field, bringing machine learning closer to practical, real-world applications. With regard to machine learning performance, our results show that OtoVision’s accuracy aligns with other studies in the field, as displayed by a previously conducted meta-analysis of tympanic membrane machine learning models [16]. However, the real test of OtoVision’s robustness and utility lies in its application in real-world scenarios, where factors such as diverse image quality and resolution come into play. Our preliminary testing suggests that the model performs well even in these scenarios, showing resilience to variations in image quality.
The integration of our model into a Rockchip RK3566 device represents a step toward bridging the gap between machine learning research and practical, user-friendly applications. Such applications have the potential to extend the reach of quality healthcare to remote and under-re- sourced areas. Furthermore, they can facilitate early and accurate disease detection, aiding prompt and effective treatment. In the next phase of this project, we plan to test

6 Conclusion
In conclusion, our study has successfully demonstrated the development and application of a machine learning model capable of classifying various ear conditions with a high degree of accuracy. The incorporation of this model into a Rockchip-powered otoscope represents a significant stride toward a cost-effective, portable, and accurate solution for ear disease diagnosis. This novel integration of machine learning and edge computing sets the foundation for a potential revolution in ear disease detection and management.
Our research underscored the model’s robustness in handling variable image resolutions and quality, a crucial attribute for its utility in real-world applications. The model’s promising performance against challenges inher- ent in telemedicine and remote healthcare settings suggests its potential as a viable diagnostic tool even in resource- constrained environments. Despite some variability in accuracy across different disease classes, the model’s overall performance surpasses or matches that of general physician diagnoses, underscoring its potential for practical deployment. The ongoing development and optimization of the OtoVision platform has the potential to significantly influence the field of otology. By increasing the accessi- bility, accuracy, and timeliness of ear disease diagnosis, OtoVision can enhance patient outcomes, particularly in underserved areas.
Furthermore, by setting a precedent for the integration of machine learning models into portable diagnostic tools, this research could inspire a new wave of innovation in medical technology, extending beyond otology to the wider landscape of healthcare. Ultimately, our hope is that Oto- Vision will not only revolutionize ear disease detection but will also contribute to the broader objective of leveraging technology to make quality healthcare accessible and affordable to all.
